title: Hosea 4:1–10
context: Chapter 4 opens a new part of Hosea. After the family narratives of chapters 1–3, the book turns to oracles in which the LORD brings “a charge against the inhabitants of the land” (4:1). The land lacks truth, goodness, and knowledge of God, and in their place stand cursing, lying, murder, stealing, and adultery, a list many readers hear as an echo of the Ten Commandments (4:2). Creation itself mourns (4:3). From verse 4 the charge narrows to the priests: the people are “destroyed for lack of knowledge” because those entrusted with God’s law rejected it, fed on the people’s sin, and left priest and people alike to be judged by their ways (4:4–10). The Hebrew of verse 4 is difficult, and readers differ on exactly who is addressed in verses 4–6. Hosea 1:1 places the prophet in the eighth century BC, in the northern kingdom, and many readers date these oracles to the unsettled decades after Jeroboam son of Joash, though the precise setting is not stated. The prostitution language that begins in verse 10 is covenant imagery for unfaithfulness to the LORD, and these notes treat it soberly. Shared ground: both traditions read the chapter as a covenant indictment, hear the LORD’s demand for real knowledge of him, and see the failure of religious leaders as especially grave.

verses.text: Hear the LORD’s word, you children of Israel, for the LORD has a charge against the inhabitants of the land: “Indeed there is no truth, nor goodness, nor knowledge of God in the land.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD brings “a charge” against the inhabitants of the land, language that many readers hear as a covenant lawsuit. Arminian readers stress that the indictment assumes real responsibility: truth, goodness, and knowledge of God are absent because the people turned from what they were given, and the charge itself is a summons to hear and respond.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the same summons and stress that the root failure is the absence of “knowledge of God,” which they read as covenant acquaintance and loyalty rather than mere information. Shared ground: both traditions read the charge as a covenant indictment, and both see truth, goodness (often understood as steadfast loyalty), and knowledge of God as the relational heart of what Israel lacked.

verses.text: There is cursing, lying, murder, stealing, and committing adultery; they break boundaries, and bloodshed causes bloodshed.
verses.arminianNotes: The list of cursing, lying, murder, stealing, and adultery recalls several of the Ten Commandments, and many readers hear Hosea deliberately echoing them (compare Exodus 20:13–16). Arminian readers emphasize that “bloodshed causes bloodshed”: sin, freely chosen, multiplies and spreads through a society that has refused correction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the list as the outward fruit of the missing knowledge of God in verse 1: when love for God is abandoned, love for neighbor collapses with it. Shared ground: both traditions read the catalog as covenant violation, not merely social disorder, and both hear in “bloodshed causes bloodshed” a picture of violence feeding on itself.

verses.text: Therefore the land will mourn, and everyone who dwells in it will waste away, with all living things in her, even the animals of the field and the birds of the sky; yes, the fish of the sea also die.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore the land will mourn.” The judgment reaches the animals of the field, the birds of the sky, and the fish of the sea. Arminian readers note that human sin has consequences for the whole created order, and that the land’s mourning displays how seriously God takes his people’s chosen unfaithfulness; some readers hear the order of creation in Genesis 1 echoed in reverse.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see creation drawn into the curse that follows covenant breaking (compare Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28), and they read the withering as God’s righteous judgment working through the natural order he governs. Shared ground: both traditions see the land’s mourning as tied to human sin, and both read creation’s suffering as a sign of the broken covenant (compare Romans 8:20–22).

verses.text: “Yet let no man bring a charge, neither let any man accuse; for your people are like those who bring charges against a priest.
verses.arminianNotes: “Yet let no man bring a charge, neither let any man accuse.” The verse is notoriously difficult, and translations differ on who is addressed. In the WEB’s rendering, the LORD silences mutual accusation among the people, because they themselves are like those who contend with a priest. Arminian readers see the LORD reserving the indictment to himself and exposing a people quick to blame others.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers, with many others, take the verse as turning the charge toward the priesthood, which becomes the focus of verses 4–10, while acknowledging that the Hebrew is hard. Shared ground: both traditions hold that the precise sense of the verse is uncertain, and both agree that the LORD alone is the rightful accuser and that no party in Israel stands blameless before him.

verses.text: You will stumble in the day, and the prophet will also stumble with you in the night; and I will destroy your mother.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD declares that the one addressed will stumble by day and the prophet by night, and “I will destroy your mother.” Arminian readers see leaders who were meant to guide the people now falling with them, so that failure in office is real and culpable. Many take “your mother” as the nation or the priest’s family, a point readers hold with caution.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that priest and prophet, the appointed channels of God’s word, are judged together, so that false religious leadership offers no shelter to anyone. Shared ground: both traditions read “your mother” with some uncertainty, whether as the nation, the priestly house, or the priest’s own family, and both see the verse as judgment on those charged with teaching.

verses.text: My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge. Because you have rejected knowledge, I will also reject you, that you may be no priest to me. Because you have forgotten your God’s law, I will also forget your children.
verses.arminianNotes: “My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge.” The LORD ties the lack to a rejection: “Because you have rejected knowledge, I will also reject you.” Arminian readers emphasize the reciprocity: this ignorance is not innocent but chosen, and the priest who forgot God’s law forfeits his calling, showing that covenant privilege can be lost when it is spurned.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that the knowledge in view is covenant knowledge entrusted to the priests, whose task was to teach the law (compare Malachi 2:7), and they read the LORD’s rejection as just judgment on willful neglect of revealed truth. Shared ground: both traditions read “lack of knowledge” as a failure of relationship and obedience, not mere lack of information, and both hear a warning to all who teach God’s people.

verses.text: As they were multiplied, so they sinned against me. I will change their glory into shame.
verses.arminianNotes: “As they were multiplied, so they sinned against me.” Growth and prosperity became occasions for more sin. Arminian readers see blessing turned to rebellion by human choice, and they read “I will change their glory into shame” as a fitting reversal that answers what the priests made of God’s gifts.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the priests’ increase in number or wealth brought no increase in faithfulness, and they see the exchange of glory for shame as God’s measured judgment (compare Psalm 106:20). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a warning that growth and privilege do not guarantee faithfulness, and both see the LORD’s response as just and proportionate.

verses.text: They feed on the sin of my people, and set their heart on their iniquity.
verses.arminianNotes: “They feed on the sin of my people.” Many take this to mean that the priests profited from the sin offerings they were permitted to eat (compare Leviticus 6:26), so they had a stake in the people’s continued sin. Arminian readers stress the corruption of a ministry that preferred gain to repentance, a free betrayal of a sacred trust.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers, reading the same likely reference to sin offerings, see a priesthood whose appetites were set “on their iniquity,” so that religious office itself became a means of sin. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an indictment of leaders who profit from the people’s failure rather than calling them to turn, and both treat the precise reference to offerings as probable rather than certain.

verses.text: It will be like people, like priest; and I will punish them for their ways, and will repay them for their deeds.
verses.arminianNotes: “It will be like people, like priest.” Arminian readers hear that office brings no immunity: the priest will be judged by the same standard as the people, and each is repaid “for their deeds,” a principle of personal accountability that runs throughout the prophets.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see priest and people bound together in one corruption, and they read “I will punish them for their ways” as God’s impartial justice, which holds leaders responsible for what they taught and modeled. Shared ground: both traditions read the proverb as leveling: neither religious status nor nearness to the sanctuary shields anyone from the LORD’s judgment on their ways and deeds.

verses.text: They will eat, and not have enough. They will play the prostitute, and will not increase; because they have abandoned listening to the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “They will eat, and not have enough. They will play the prostitute, and will not increase.” Arminian readers see futility as the consequence of having “abandoned listening to the LORD”: what people pursue apart from God cannot satisfy. The prostitution language is covenant imagery for unfaithfulness and may also allude to fertility rites, though that is debated.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress the root cause the verse names, abandoning the LORD, and see the frustrated appetite as God’s judgment on trust placed in other sources of fertility and plenty. Shared ground: both traditions read the imagery soberly as covenant unfaithfulness, and both see the futility curses (compare Leviticus 26:26) as fitting consequences of turning away from the LORD.
